summary: Improper role-based-access control in Langfuse LLM connection management allowed users of role “member” to retrieve stored LLM provider API keys
description:
**Affected versions**
Self-hosted: >= 3.68.0, < 3.167.0
Cloud: Deployed versions prior to April 9, 2026, 1PM UTC 

**Patched versions**
Self-hosted: >= 3.167.0
Cloud: Patched since April 9, 2026, 1PM UTC 

**Summary**
Langfuse Cloud prior to April 9, 2026, 1PM UTC and self-hosted versions before 3.167.0 contained a role-based-access control flaw in the LLM connection update flow. 

An authenticated, low-privileged user of role “member” in a project could request the update of an existing LLM connection to an attacker-controlled `baseUrl`, causing Langfuse to reuse the stored provider secret and redirect the test request to an attacker-controlled endpoint. 

This could expose the plaintext provider LLM API key for that connection.
**The attack is only possible if a user is already part of a project and has “member” scoped access.**

**What users need to know**
If you run a vulnerable self-hosted Langfuse version and invite untrusted users with ‘member’ permissions into projects with configured LLM connections, a user of role “member” in the same project may have been able to retrieve stored LLM provider credentials, such as OpenAI API keys, from those connections.

Note that this attack is only possible if a user is already part of a project and has “member” scoped access. **The attack is not possible for other users of different organizations or projects or anonymous users.**

**Attack vector**
The issue was in the authenticated LLM connection update flow that tested the updated connection against the provided endpoint.

A low-privileged authenticated user of role “member” with access to the same project could:
1. Access the project settings of the given project and edit an existing LLM connection
2. Supply an attacker-controlled `baseURL` in the update form
4. Omit a new secret so the server reused the stored secret for the saved connection.
5. Capture the outbound authorization header when Langfuse performed the connection test

**Impact**
Successful exploitation could disclose stored LLM provider credentials for existing connections in the same project. An attacker with the exposed credential could then use the affected upstream provider account within the limits of that credential.

**Recommended immediate actions**
Upgrade to Langfuse 3.167.0 or later.
Rotate stored LLM provider API keys for sensitive projects with untrusted project members
Review project membership and remove untrusted users from projects containing shared LLM credentials.

**Workarounds**
If you cannot upgrade immediately:
do not store high-value shared LLM provider credentials in projects accessible to untrusted members
restrict Langfuse outbound egress so connection tests cannot reach arbitrary external hosts

**Timeline**
March 31, 2026: security researchers reach out and share reproduction steps of this vulnerability involving the loopback host, which initially led to incorrect triaging of this issue as a non-vulnerability
April 8, 2026: Upon further investigation by a Langfuse engineer that picked up this incorrectly low-prioritized report, this vulnerability was reproduced
April 9, 2026: Vulnerability was patched, and fixes were deployed to Langfuse Cloud and in patched releases for self-host/OSS ([v3.167.0](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v3.167.0)).
April 16, 2025: CVE published after advance notice period for enterprise self-hosted customers

**Pull requests with patches:** 
https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/pull/13027
https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/pull/13055

**Credits**
We thank the reporting security researchers, [Quốc Anh Đỗ](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anhdq201/), [Khanh Nguyen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/com0tf3/), and [Mustafa Bilgici](https://github.com/MustafaBilgici)  for responsibly disclosing this issue.

summary: Unauthenticated Slack OAuth Install Allows Linking Slack to Arbitrary Project Improper Access Control)
description:
This vulnerability was identified by [Aikido Attack](https://www.aikido.dev/attack/aipentest).

## Summary

The `/api/public/slack/install` endpoint initiates Slack OAuth using a projectId provided by the client without authentication or authorization. Combined with the callback storing installations by untrusted metadata, an attacker can bind their Slack workspace to any project and possibly receive changes to Prompts stored in Langfuse Prompt Management. No data captured in Langfuse Tracing or LLM-as-a-Judge is transmitted to the Slack Integration.

The vulnerability has not been exploited on Langfuse Cloud based on our review of logs.

## Details

The [Slack integration](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/webhooks-slack-integrations) exposes a public installation flow that solely relies on the projectId passed as the query parameter and it is preserved throughout the OAuth authentication flow. At the end of the authentication flow, the provided project is connected with the Slack workspace.  
This trust in client-controlled metadata creates an insecure path: any unauthenticated user who knows or guesses a valid projectId can initiate Slack OAuth and, upon completion in a properly configured environment, link their Slack workspace to the victim’s project, potentially exfiltrating notifications or automation outputs.  
Using the unsecured API, the attacker can create or update Slack Integrations. He is not able to configure [Prompt Automations](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/webhooks-slack-integrations) which is required so that Langfuse sends data to the malicious Slack integration. Thus, there are two different ways on how the vulnerability could lead to exposed Prompts:

* A Project does have a Prompt Slack Automation set up already. In this case, the attacker could replace the user-configured Slack integration with an attacker-configured Slack integration.  
* A project does not have a Prompt Slack Automation set up. An attacker could create a Slack integration which has no immediate effect. An authenticated user with access to the project could then set up the Prompt Slack integration using the attackers Slack integration. This is unlikely to happen as we show the Slack Workspace name alongside the Slack Team Id in the UI before setting up the automation. Also, users need to select a specific channel where to send the Prompts to. Missing or unfamiliar channels would likely make the user aware of an issue.

## Proof of Concept

**Step 1: Link attacker’s Slack workspace to a victim project**

1. Open an incognito browser session.  
2. Visit the following URL with a valid victim projectId: `https://<langfuse-url>/api/public/slack/install?projectId=my-project`  
2. Click “Add to Slack” and complete the OAuth flow using the attacker’s Slack workspace.

After the OAuth flow completes, the Slack workspace is linked to the victim project without requiring any Langfuse authentication.

**Step 2: Receive victim prompt updates**

- If the victim project already has a Prompt Slack Automation configured, Langfuse will start sending prompt updates to the attacker’s Slack workspace.  
- Otherwise, the attacker’s Slack integration remains attached to the project and may later be selected by a legitimate user when configuring Prompt Slack Automations.

This results in Langfuse-managed Prompts being delivered to the attacker-controlled Slack workspace.

## Impact

If you do not use [Prompt Automations with Slack](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/webhooks-slack-integrations), you are not affected. In the case of a successful attack, Langfuse sends Langfuse managed Prompts to the attackers Slack. No tracing data or LLM-as-a-Judge data is affected which should rule our PII impact in most deployments.

## Remediation

Review the Slack integration in your project settings and ensure that you own and control the Slack workspace being referenced. Optionally, you can re-connect your Slack workspace from the project settings.

## Timeline

- January 14th, 2026 09:42 GMT: GitHub vulnerability submission.  
- January 15th, 2026 07:59 GMT: Langfuse team [patched](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/pull/11566) vulnerability on Langfuse Cloud.  
- January 15th, 2026 10:45 GMT: Langfuse team validates that an exploit on Langfuse Cloud is highly unlikely by reviewing database state and access logs.  
- January 15th, 2026 10:07 GMT: Langfuse publishes a [patched release](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v3.147.0) for OSS/self-hosted users.

summary: SSO Account Takeover via CSRF or phishing attack
description:
## Description

For SSO provider configurations without an explicit `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_CHECK` setting, a potential account takeover may happen if an authenticated user is made to call a specifically crafted URL via a CSRF or phishing attack.

## Impact

If an authenticated user is tricked or coerced into the call of a specifically crafted URL (a modified version of the \`/api/auth/callback/{provider}\` endpoint), e.g. through phishing or CSRF, the attacker's SSO account can be linked with the victim account. In this case, the attacker can act as the victim going forward.

Langfuse Cloud: Enterprise SSO is not affected as it sets these checks by default. “Sign in with Google, AzureAD, GitHub” was affected but not actively exploited based on an analysis of the active Langfuse Cloud database state.

Self-hosted: If `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_CHECK` is set to `pkce,state` the vulnerability cannot be exploited. Multiple Enterprise SSO platforms, e.g. Okta, reject authentication requests without setting `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_CHECK` to pkce, thus, we conclude that many deployments will have this configured correctly.

## Conditions Required for Exploitation

- An SSO provider is configured without setting `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_CHECK`  
- The attacker must start an SSO session with Langfuse, and abort the authentication flow after the callback URL was generated by their identity provider. They must not follow the redirect using this callback URL to Langfuse.  
- The attacker tricks a user who is signed into Langfuse to perform a GET request to the Langfuse callback URl with the attacker's authentication code. The specific request depends on the identity provider, but generally follows the `GET /api/auth/callback/{provider}` pattern.

## Patches

- Langfuse Cloud (EU, US, HIPAA): Affected until checks were set explicitly on November 12th, 2025\.  
- Self-hosted versions which contain patches: \>=3.131.0, \>=2.95.12

## Workarounds

Set `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_CHECK`. We recommend setting `pkce,state`.

## Timeline

- November 12, 2025 11:42 UTC: Security researcher submits vulnerability to [security@langfuse.com](mailto:security@langfuse.com)  
- November 12, 2025 13:16 UTC: Langfuse team patches vulnerability on Langfuse Cloud.  
- November 12, 2025 14:37 UTC: Langfuse [releases](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v3.17.0) a patched release for OSS/self-hosted users.  
- November 12, 2025 15:14 UTC: Langfuse concludes that no Cloud environment has any non-expired, dual SSO account links to user accounts which indicates no active exploits of the given vulnerability.

summary: Cross‑organization enumeration of member & invitation lists via project membership APIs
description:
In certain project membership APIs, the server trusted a user‑controlled orgId and used it in authorization checks. As a result, any authenticated user on the same Langfuse instance could enumerate names and email addresses of users in another organization if they knew the target organization’s ID.
APIs:
- `/api/trpc/members.allFromProject` (members listing)
- `/api/trpc/members.allInvitesFromProject` (outstanding invitations) 

### Impact
Disclosure is limited to names and email addresses of members/invitees. No customer data such as traces, prompts, or evaluations is exposed or accessible.
For Langfuse Cloud, we ran a thorough investigation of access logs of the last 30 days and could not find any evidence that this vulnerability was exploited.
For most self-hosting deployments, the attack surface is significantly reduced given an SSO provider is configured and email/password sign-up is disabled ([self-hosted authentication documentation](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/security/authentication-and-sso)). In these cases, only users who authenticate via the Enterprise SSO IdP (e.g. Okta) would be able to exploit this vulnerability to access the member list, i.e. internal users getting access to a list of other internal users.

### Conditions Required for Exploitation
- The actor must have a valid Langfuse user account within the same instance.
- The actor must know the target orgId.
- The actor must use the request made to the API that powers the frontend membership tables, including their project/user authentication token, while changing the orgId to the target organization.

### Patches
- Langfuse Cloud (EU, US, HIPAA): Affected until fix deployment on November 1, 2025. We reviewed the Langfuse Cloud access logs from the past 30 days and found no evidence that this vulnerability was exploited.
- Self-Hosted versions which contain patches: 
  - Major version 2: >= [v2.95.11](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v2.95.11)
  - Major version 3: >= [v3.124.1](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v3.124.1)

### Workarounds
There are no known workarounds. Upgrading is required to fully mitigate this issue.


### References
- Fix commit 1:[ https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/commit/6c2529049a4c962928c435984c81a547a497e3e5](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/commit/6c2529049a4c962928c435984c81a547a497e3e5)
- Fix commit 2:[ https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/commit/67990ebfdcf0f0c32a6710efa7ddbda073812ab4](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/commit/67990ebfdcf0f0c32a6710efa7ddbda073812ab4)
- Langfuse release which introduced the vulnerability: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v2.70.0

### Timeline of Events
- Nov 1, 2025: security researcher reaches out and shares details regarding this vulnerability
- Nov 1-2, 2025: Langfuse reproduced the vulnerabilities, patched them, deployed fixes to Langfuse Cloud, and released patched releases for self-host/OSS ([v3.124.1](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v3.124.1)).
- Nov 2, 2025: Langfuse concluded investigation that the vulnerability has not been exploited within the last 30 days on Langfuse Cloud
- Nov 5, 2025: We released a patch for Langfuse v2. We delayed this release because v2 is no longer maintained, and updates for v2 can increase awareness of the vulnerability.
- Nov 9, 2025: CVE published after advance notice period for enterprise self-hosted customers



Reported by: Team DisclosureX
